Copper-catalysed asymmetric 
hydroboration of alkenes with 
1,2-benzazaborines to access chiral 
naphthalene isosteres
Wanlan Su    1, Jide Zhu1, Yu Chen2, Xu Zhang1, Weihua Qiu1, Kai Yang    1 , 
Peiyuan Yu    2  & Qiuling Song    1 
Bioisosteric replacement has emerged as a clear strategy for 
drug-structure optimization. Naphthalene is the core element of many 
chiral pharmaceuticals and drug candidates. However, as a promising 
isostere of naphthalene, the chiral version of 1,2-benzazaborine has 
rarely been explored due to the lack of efficient synthetic methods. 
Here we describe a copper-catalysed enantioselective hydroboration 
of alkenes with 1,2-benzazaborines. The method provides a general 
platform for the atom-economic and efficient construction of diverse 
chiral 1,2-benzazaborine compounds (more than 60 examples) that bear a 
2-carbon-stereogenic centre or allene skeleton in high yields and excellent 
enantioselectivities. T hr ee 1 ,2 -b en za za borine analogues of bioactive 
chiral naphthalene-containing molecules have been prepared, and a 
series of transformations around c hi ral 1 ,2 -b en za za borines have also been 
developed. Notably, the hydroboration process of this study reveals that the 
identity of 1  , 2  -b  e n  za  z a borine plays an essential role in the rate-determining 
step and catalyst resting state.
Bioisosteric replacement is an important strategy for drug discovery 
that has been widely practised by medicinal chemists1,2. Such a strategy 
can not only improve the physicochemical properties of lead mol -
ecules, but can also expand intellectual property space. Naphthalene 
is a ubiquitous pharmacophore present in many bioactive molecules 
with anticancer, anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial and antiviral activi-
ties, and so on3. In recent years, 1,2-benzazaborines have attracted 
considerable interest as naphthalene replacements4–8 (Fig. 1a), and 
often exhibit better bioactivity than their all-carbon equivalents, 
probably because the NH groups of the 1,2-benzazaborines can act 
as hydrogen-bond donors for better binding to proteins9–12 (Fig. 1b). 
Furthermore, the introduction of three-dimensional elements into 
flat molecules often acts to improve biological activities and physi-
cal properties13,14. Naphthalene-containing chiral molecules have a 
place in marketed pharmaceuticals and drug candidates 3 (Fig. 1c). 
However, similar molecules with isosteric 1,2-benzazaborines have 
not been explored because of a lack of efficient methods to assemble 
such molecules with three-dimensional shape.
Although many direct-synthesis or late-modification methods 
have been developed to construct substituted 1,2-benzazaborines, the 
methods for preparing chiral 1,2-benzazaborines are extremely lim -
ited15–18. The common method for the preparation of 1,2-benzazaborines 
involves an annulation/aromatization reaction of trifluoroborates and 
2-aminostyrenes19. However, the methodology is unlikely to provide

Results and discussion
We first investigated this envisioned asymmetric hydroboration reac-
tion using 4-fluorostyrene (1a) and 1,2-benzazaborine (2a) as test 
substrates. As shown in Table 1, a wide range of bisphosphine ligands 
were investigated for their efficiency to promote the reaction. Pleas-
ingly, the desired product 3a was obtained in 49% NMR yield and 80% 
e.e. with CuCl as catalyst and (R,R)-Me-Duphos (L1) as ligand (Table 1, 
entry 1). This result proved the feasibility of this enantioselective hyd-
roboration using 1,2-benzazaborine as the boron reagent and encour-
aged us to further investigate other ligands (Table 1 , entries 2–8). 
(S,S,S,S)-MeO-BIBOP (L2), (R,Sp)-Josiphos (L3) and (S)-QuinoxP (L4) 
were inefficient in this transformation (Table 1, entries 2–4). Axially 
chiral bisphosphine ligands (S)-BINAP (L5) and (R)-Segphos (L6) were 
almost useless for this reaction (entries 5 and 6). Interestingly, sterically 
bulky (R)-DM-Segphos (L7) and (S)-DTBM-Segphos (L8) were appro-
priate ligands in terms of both their reaction efficiency and excellent 
stereocontrol, giving chiral 1,2-benzazaborine 3a in 65% yield and 93% 
e.e. (entry 7) and 89% yield and >99% e.e. (entry 8), respectively. L8 was 
determined to be the best ligand. Slightly increasing the amount of 
1,2-benzazaborine provided optimal conditions for this transformation, 
affording the desired product 3a in 94% yield and >99% e.e. (entry 9). A 
control experiment revealed that the catalytic amount of NaOtBu was 
critical for the formation of the desired product (entry 10).
Having optimized the model asymmetric hydroboration of 
4-fluorostyrene with 1,2-benzazaborine, we investigated the substrate 
scope starting with a diverse range of styrenes (Table 2). Variation of 
the para-substituted styrenes (3a–3i) had little effect on enantiose -
lectivity (96–99% e.e.) for this asymmetric hydroboration reaction, 
but electron-rich substituents reduced the reactivity (3e and 3f). The 
absolute configuration of 3b was determined by X-ray crystallographic 
analysis (CCDC 2245401). It is worth mentioning that the alkynyl group 
was tolerated well in moderate yield (3i) without additional hydrobo-
ration of the alkyne. Various ortho- and meta-substituted styrenes 
general access to chiral 1,2-benzazaborines due to the lower yields for 
alkyl trifluoroborates19, as well as owing to the fact that complex chiral 
trifluoroborates are difficult to synthesize20. A direct asymmetric cata-
lytic strategy for the assembly of such molecules is a much more attrac-
tive and promising approach. The catalytic asymmetric hydroboration 
reaction has emerged as a synthetic toolbox to prepare chiral organo-
boron compounds21–41, and we wondered whether such asymmetric 
hydroboration between alkenes and 1,2-benzazaborines could be used 
to construct chiral 1,2-benzazaborines. Of note, as an important type 
of borane, B–H bond activation of 1,2-azaborines involving transition 
metals has been studied less 18,42, and the corresponding hydrobora -
tion reaction has not yet been explored. One main reason might lie 
in the fact that 1,2-azaborines are more stable than other traditional 
boranes, such as BH3, 9-borabicyclo[3.3.1]nonane (9-BBN), pinacolbo-
rane (HBpin), catecholborane (HBCat) and 2,3-dihydro-1H-naphtho[1,
8-de][1,3,2]diazaborinine (HBdan)43. As evidence, the aforementioned 
traditional boranes readily react with active protons to release H 2, 
whereas 1,2-azaborines are relatively stable in acidic environments18. 
Therefore, direct activation of the B–H bond in 1,2-azaborines is a big 
challenge in boron chemistry, and the successful transformations of 
this bond will greatly enrich boron chemistry and enhance the utiliza-
tion of 1,2-azaborines in various fields.
In this Article we describe a simple approach to chiral 
1,2-benzazaborines that exploits an asymmetric hydroboration 
between alkenes and 1,2-benzazaborines (Fig. 1d). This chemistry 
enables a general and atom-economic preparation of a wide range 
of chiral 1,2-benzazaborines bearing an α-carbon-stereogenic cen -
tre in high yields and excellent enantioselectivities. Moreover, this 
protocol can also be extended to the efficient preparation of chiral 
1,2-benzazaborines with an allene skeleton as well as chiral gem-diboryl 
alkanes. We believe that our strategy will greatly expand the range of 
chiral organoborons and provide alternative skeletons and efficient 
methods for medicinal chemistry as well as pharmaceuticals.

(3j–3m) were investigated next, and these were also smoothly hydrobo-
rated. Strong electron-deficient substituents (3k, 3l) and ortho-OMe 
(3m) had a minimal influence on the reactivity and enantioselectivities. 
There was a low yield of para-OMe (3e), but ortho-OMe (3m) may coor-
dinate with the alkyl copper intermediate, resulting in easy insertion 
of Cu–H species and good yield (35% versus 83%). 2-Vinylnaphthalene 
was also a suitable candidate for this reaction (3n, 99% yield, 98% 
e.e.). Vinyl-substituted heteroaromatics including benzothiophen 
(3o), benzofuran (3p), indole (3q ) and thiophene (3r) all furnished 
the hydroborated products in moderate to high yields with excellent 
enantioselectivities (all 98% e.e.). T o our delight, diverse β-substituted 
styrenes (internal alkenes) were also aptly transformed, providing 
α-selective borated products (3s–3x) in moderate to good yields with 
good to excellent enantioselectivities (53–92% yields, up to >99% e.e.). 
However, β,β-disubstituted styrenes exhibited low reactivity under 
standard conditions, probably due to difficulty in the addition of Cu–H 
to the more sterically encumbered olefin. Moreover, this reaction also 
tolerated more substituted 1,2-benzazaborines (Table 2), affording the 
enantiopure 1,2-benzazaborine products with excellent enantiose -
lectivities (3y–3aj, 98% to >99% e.e.). It was found that the electronic 
property and position of substituents on the 1,2-benzazaborines had 
little effect on enantioselectivities. Of note, installation of the sub -
stituents on the nitrogen atom greatly affected the efficiency of the 
reaction; the corresponding hydroboration products 3ai and 3aj were 
obtained in 70% yield and 98% e.e. and 37% yield and 98% e.e., respec-
tively, illustrating the steric influence of the substituents of the nitrogen 
atom on the yield.
Having established robust reactivity for the asymmetric hydrobo-
ration of styrenes, we next turned our attention to explore the enanti-
oselective hydroboration of alkenyl borons (Table 2). A wide range of 
alkenyl borons could be used as suitable substrates for this addition 
reaction to deliver the corresponding enantiopure gem-diboryl alkanes 
with excellent enantioselectivities (4a–4i, 91–98% e.e.). The hydrobo-
ration was highly regioselective and only installed 1,2-benzazaborine 
onto the α-carbon of the boryl group in alkenyl borons. The enantio-
pure 1,2-benzazaborine containing an α-Bpin group has the potential 
for further modifications 28,44–47. Encouraged by the success of the 
enantioselective hydroboration of alkenyl Bpins, the elusive alkenyl 
1,2-benzazaborine substrates were then explored to examine the poten-
tial of generating chiral gem-di-1,2-benzazaborines. Unlike alkenyl 
Bpins, the asymmetric addition of alkenyl 1,2-azaborine has not yet 
been reported. T o our surprise, the alkenyl 1,2-benzazaborines could 
also undergo hydroboration with high efficiency and excellent enan-
tioselectivities to furnish chiral gem-di-1,2-benzazaborines 4h (77% 
yield, 98% e.e.) and 4i (87% yield, 98% e.e.).
Having investigated the synthesis of centrally chiral 1,2-  
benzazaborines, we were interested in exploring the asymmetric hyd-
roboration of 1,3-enynes to access chiral 1,2-benzazaborines with allene 
skeletons, because allene units are commonly found in natural prod-
ucts, bioactive molecules and materials48–51. The enantiopure allenyl 
1,2-benzazaborines could be obtained by further simple optimization of 
the conditions. As shown in Table 2, aryl-, alkenyl- and alkyl-substituted 
1,3-enynes could all undergo the asymmetric hydroboration reaction 
with 1,2-benzazaborines to generate the corresponding chiral allenyl 
1,2-benzazaborine products (5a–5g) in excellent enantioselectivities 
(97% to >99% e.e.). As can be seen from Table 2, the mild conditions of 
the asymmetric hydroboration with 1,2-benzazaborines could tolerate 
diverse functional groups, including halogens (3a–3c, 3j, 3t, 3ab–3ae, 
3ai, 4d, 4i and 5c), ether (3e, 3h, 3m, 3z, 3aa, 4b and 5a), ester (3f, 3l, 
3aj, 4c, 4e and 5g), alkyne (3i), alkene (5e) and imido (5f). The absolute 
configuration of 5b was determined by computational and experimen-
tal circular dichroism spectroscopy (Supplementary Fig. 1).
The high functional group tolerance prompted us to explore the 
utility of late-stage modification of biorelevant molecules (Fig. 2a). A 
series of bioactive molecules (oestrone, ezetimibe, clofibrate, gemfi-
brozil, cholesterol and l-menthol) were derivatized into their corre-
sponding alkenes, which, following treatment with 1,2-benzazaborine 
(2a) under established asymmetric hydroboration conditions, were 
smoothly transformed into eventual chiral 1,2-benzazaborine deriva-
tives 6a–6f with excellent enantioselectivities. The stability of these 
compounds in air and aqueous conditions was also tested (Supple -
mentary Fig. 3). As isosteres of naphthalene, bioactive molecular 
analogues 8, 10 and 12 (refs. 52–54 ) containing 1,2-benzazaborines 
could be efficiently synthesized, indicating that this process may be 
applicable in drug discovery (Fig. 2b ). In addition, further synthetic 
transformations of the chiral 1,2-benzazaborine products were then 
explored. First, product 3v could be iodinated to deliver product 13, 
and further cross-coupling with organozinc reagents could afford the 
corresponding 3-arylation product 14  and 3-alkylation product 15

The general copper-catalysed hydroboration process includes 
alkene insertion into L*Cu–H species, and σ-bond metathesis between 
the resulting L*Cu–alkyl intermediate and borane to generate the 
product and regenerate the L*Cu–H species56. T o gain a deeper insight 
into the mechanism of this asymmetric hydroboration reaction, a 
series of experiments were carried out. T o achieve better experi -
mental reproducibility, the initial rates of the reaction used CuO tBu 
as catalyst. For the hydroboration of NH-1,2-benzazaborine (2a), 
the experimental results showed that the reaction was first-order 
with respect to alkene 1a and the Cu-catalyst, indicating that the 
alkene insertion into L*Cu–H species was probably the rate-limiting 
step (Fig. 3a ; details are provided in Supplementary Figs. 4–6). A 
negative order (−0.6 order) was found with respect to borane 2a, 
which suppressed the alkene insertion process, possibly due to the 
formation of a resting-state complex between the L*Cu–H species and 
borane 2a (Fig. 3a). The generation of such a copper–dihydridobo -
ron complex 1_H (resting-state complex) was further verified by 11B 
NMR spectroscopy (details are provided in Supplementary Fig. 10). 
Interestingly, for the hydroboration of N-Me-1,2-benzazaborine (2l), 
the reaction was zero-order in alkene 1a and first-order in borane 
2l and the Cu catalyst (Fig. 3b ; details are provided in Supplemen -
tary Figs. 7–9), indicating that the σ-bond metathesis between the 
L*Cu–alkyl intermediate and borane 2l was the rate-determining 
step. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed 
to further investigate the mechanism of this reaction (Fig. 3c ). For 
NH-1,2-benzazaborine ( 2a), from the resting state 1_H, the active 
L*Cu–H species is formed by releasing a 1,2-benzazaborine molecule 
in an endergonic process (4.4 kcal mol−1). Subsequently, alkene inser-
tion into the L*Cu–H species occurs via the favourable transition state 
TS1-R to generate the L*Cu–alkyl intermediate Int1-R . This process 
needs to overcome a free energy barrier of 12.2 kcal mol −1 relative 
to 1_H. Finally, product 3a is formed by σ-bond metathesis between 
Int1-R  and 2a via transition state H- TS2-R , which has a free energy 
barrier of 10.6 kcal mol −1. Meanwhile, for N-Me-1,2-benzazaborine 
(2l), from the copper–dihydridoboron complex 1_Me to the transi-
tion state TS1-R  of alkene insertion there is a free energy barrier of 
10.9 kcal mol −1. Subsequent σ-bond metathesis occurs via transi -
tion state Me- TS2-R  with a free energy barrier of 11.8 kcal mol −1, 
to give final product 3ai. The calculated results indicate that the 
rate-determining steps are respectively alkene insertion and 
σ-bond metathesis for substrates NH-1,2-benzazaborine (2a) and 
N-Me-1,2-benzazaborine (2l), consistent with the experimental 
observations. The switch in the relative magnitude of these two bar -
riers is a combined result due to the reduced stability of the copper–
dihydridoboron complex (from −4.4 to −3.1 kcal mol −1) and a slight 
increase (from 10.6 to 11.8 kcal mol −1) in the σ-bond metathesis for 
the N-Me-substituted 1,2-benzazaborine substrate 2l. These results 
also show that the identity of 1,2-benzazaborine plays a decisive 
role in the rate-determining step and catalyst resting state. On the 
basis of the above results and previous reports 56, a catalytic cycle is 
proposed, as shown in Fig. 3d.
In conclusion, we have developed a copper-catalysed enan -
tioselective hydroboration reaction to access enantioenriched 
2-substituted-1,2-benzazaborine compounds from a variety of alkenes 
and 1,2-benzazaborines. The value of this chemistry was further proven 
by late-stage modification of complex molecules, the synthesis of 
bioactive molecular analogues and derivatization of the resulting prod-
ucts. It is expected that this B–H bond activation of 1,2-benzazaborines 
will be applicable to diverse enantioselective transformations, thereby 
allowing 1,2-azaborines to serve as progenitors to chiral arene isosteres 
of broad interest.

Methods
General procedure for the asymmetric hydroboration  
reaction of alkenes
In a glove box filled with high-purity argon, a 10-ml Young tube was 
charged with CuCl (0.6 mg, 3 mol%), (S )-DTBM-Segphos (7.8 mg, 
3.3 mol%), NaOtBu (1.2 mg, 6 mol%) and 0.8 ml of toluene, then the mix-
ture was stirred for 10 min. After that, a solution of 1,2-benzazaborines 
2 (0.3 mmol, 1.5 equiv.) in 0.4 ml of toluene was injected into the Young 
tube and stirred for 10 min. Finally, a solution of alkenes (0.2 mmol, 
1 equiv.) in 0.4 ml of toluene was added. The tube was removed from 
the glove box and stirred at room temperature (28–36 °C). Upon 
completion, proper amount of silica gel was added to the reaction 
mixture. After removal of the solvent, the crude reaction mixture was 
purified on silica gel (petroleum ether and ethyl acetate) to afford the 
desired products.
General procedure for the asymmetric hydroboration 
reaction of 1,3-enynes
In a glove box filled with high-purity argon, a 10-ml Young tube was 
charged with CuOAc (1.8 mg, 5 mol%), (S,S)-Ph-BPE (6.0 mg, 6 mol%) 
and 0.8 ml of hexane, then the mixture was stirred for 10 min. After that, 
a solution of 1,2-benzazaborines 2  (0.3 mmol, 1.5 equiv.) in 0.2 ml of 
toluene was injected into the Young tube, and stirred for 10 min. Finally, 
a solution of 1,3-enynes (0.2 mmol, 1 equiv.) in 0.8 ml of hexane was 
added. The tube was removed from the glove box and stirred at room 
temperature (28–36 °C). Upon completion, a proper amount of silica 
gel was added to the reaction mixture. After removal of the solvent, the 
crude reaction mixture was purified on silica gel (petroleum ether and 
ethyl acetate) to afford the desired products.
